clue.text: Rascal is confounded by Richardson heroine

indicators.note: confounded means thrown into confusion, so the letters of the two words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A scoundrel bewilders a novel's leading lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is confounded' signals the anagram of RASCAL plus the 'is' at its head; Clarissa is the title heroine of Samuel Richardson's epistolary novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa Harlowe is the heroine of Samuel Richardson's novel Clarissa, so she is a Richardson heroine by name.

clue.text: Bloom makes lion quiet (a bit long in the tooth)

parts.note: Leo is the lion of the zodiac
p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

parts.words: a bit long in the tooth
parts.note: someone a bit long in the tooth is old

explanation.surface: A flower makes a big cat fall silent, the beast being rather elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloom' looks like a flower; it is Leopold Bloom, the hero of Joyce's Ulysses.
explanation.definitionFit: Leopold is the first name of Bloom, the advertising canvasser who wanders Dublin in Joyce's Ulysses.

clue.text: Changing form of work, and getting new actors

explanation.surface: A theatre company reshapes a production and hires a fresh company.
explanation.definitionFit: Recasting is reshaping something, such as metal or a piece of writing, and also giving a play's roles to different players.

clue.text: County with terrible ogres,

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'County with terrible ogres,' (6): it ends on a comma and no word or wordplay leads to SUSSEX; the rest of the clue is missing and a search did not find it.

clue.text: King with two writers suggests Thackeray character

parts.note: Arthur is the legendary king of Camelot
a pen is a writer, the instrument one writes with
John Dennis was an English critic and playwright of the early eighteenth century

explanation.surface: A monarch flanked by two authors hints at a figure from a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The two writers are a pen, the tool, and Dennis, the critic John Dennis whom Pope mocked; Arthur Pendennis is the hero of Thackeray's Pendennis.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Pendennis is the young hero of Thackeray's novel Pendennis and narrator of The Newcomes.

clue.text: Boxer and professor using some pretty gamy cusswords

indicators.note: using some of the words means only a run of their letters is taken

explanation.surface: A fighter and an academic resort to rather foul language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'using some' takes a run from 'gamy cusswords'. Amycus was the king of the Bebryces who challenged all comers to box and was beaten by Polydeuces; Amycus Carrow is a Death Eater who teaches at Hogwarts.
explanation.definitionFit: Amycus names both a mythical boxer slain by the Argonaut Polydeuces and Professor Carrow in the Harry Potter books.

clue.text: Granted, like Capote's petitions

explanation.surface: Truman Capote's requests were fulfilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Prayers that are granted have been met, and Answered Prayers is the title of Truman Capote's unfinished novel.

clue.text: I back him at a rebus or a against the best rhymer in the kingdom" (Sheridan, School for Scandal)

definitions.text: I back him at a rebus or a against the best rhymer in the kingdom" (Sheridan, School for Scandal)

parts.words: I back him at a rebus or a against the best rhymer in the kingdom" (Sheridan, School for Scandal)
parts.note: a quotation with one word left out after 'or a': the missing word is a party word game set beside the rebus

explanation.surface: A line from Sheridan's comedy with a word gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In The School for Scandal Sir Benjamin Backbite's uncle boasts 'I'll back him at a rebus or a charade against the best rhymer in the kingdom'; the solver supplies the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A word game in which syllables are acted or hinted at, the natural partner of a rebus in a list of parlour puzzles.

clue.text: Coleridge wrote his manual

parts.note: the clue asks whose manual Coleridge wrote, pointing to the title of his 1816 lay sermon

explanation.surface: A poet wrote someone's handbook.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's lay sermon of 1816 is The Statesman's Manual; 'his' stands for the politician of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge addressed The Statesman's Manual to the governing classes, so the man is a political leader.

clue.text: Longfellow's were nocturnal

parts.note: points to Longfellow's first collection of verse, named for sounds of the night

explanation.surface: Longfellow's somethings came out after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's first book of poems (1839) was Voices of the Night.
explanation.definitionFit: The title Voices of the Night makes Longfellow's spoken sounds belong to the night.

clue.text: Stevenson in Samoa

parts.note: asks what Robert Louis Stevenson was called by the Samoans among whom he spent his last years

explanation.surface: The author living out his days in the South Seas.
explanation.walkthrough: The Samoans called Robert Louis Stevenson Tusitala, 'teller of tales'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tusitala, Samoan for storyteller, was the name the islanders gave Robert Louis Stevenson.

clue.text: Painter well versed in French customs

explanation.surface: An artist who knows all about the habits of France.
explanation.walkthrough: Henri Rousseau was the painter; the second reading points to Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who wrote on French manners and society, with 'well versed' also hinting at the poet Jean-Baptiste Rousseau.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Rousseau, 'Le Douanier', painted jungle scenes, and his nickname means customs officer; Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote at length on society and manners.

clue.text: Galsworthy's getaway

parts.note: names Galsworthy's 1926 play about a convict on the run

explanation.surface: The novelist's breakout.
explanation.walkthrough: Escape is John Galsworthy's 1926 play about a man who breaks out of Dartmoor prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A getaway is a flight from confinement, and that is the title of Galsworthy's play.

clue.text: Bennett's man followed by Ali with weapon

definitions.text: Bennett's man followed by Ali with weapon

parts.words: Bennett's man followed by Ali with weapon
parts.note: Ali was born Cassius Clay and a hanger is a short sword, so the surname following the first name is Clayhanger

explanation.surface: Arnold Bennett's hero comes after the boxer and his sword.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Bennett's hero is Edwin Clayhanger: the first name is followed by CLAY (Muhammad Ali's birth name) plus HANGER, a short sword.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin Clayhanger is the title character of Arnold Bennett's novel Clayhanger, set in the Potteries.

clue.text: Goethe's assistant has a part in a three decker Mann wrote

indicators.note: the name sits as a part inside the run of words that follows, taking letters across them

explanation.surface: Goethe's secretary appears in a long novel by Thomas Mann.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has a part in' points inside 'decker Mann'; a three-decker is a long three-volume novel, the sort Thomas Mann wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Peter Eckermann was Goethe's secretary and recorded his Conversations with Goethe.

clue.text: Spy genre pioneer might be hep in poem

indicators.note: these words could become the name if rearranged, so the phrase after the indicator is jumbled

explanation.surface: A thriller writer could turn up, fashionably, in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges HEP IN POEM. E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote early spy thrillers such as The Great Impersonation.
explanation.definitionFit: E. Phillips Oppenheim was among the first novelists of international espionage, writing over a hundred thrillers.

clue.text: Bradbury's lineage?

parts.note: a lineage is a family tree, and Ray Bradbury wrote a book called The somethingTree

explanation.surface: Asks about Ray Bradbury's family history.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray Bradbury wrote The Halloween Tree; a family tree is a lineage, so his 'lineage' is that tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark admits the stretch: Bradbury's book title names a tree, and a family tree is a lineage.

clue.text: A verse form of Bentley / Quite evidently. And, as many agree, / Not improved on by me

definitions.text: A verse form of Bentley / Quite evidently. And, as many agree, / Not improved on by me

parts.words: A verse form of Bentley / Quite evidently. And, as many agree, / Not improved on by me
parts.note: the clue itself is a comic four-line biographical verse, the form E. C. Bentley invented

explanation.surface: A setter's own comic quatrain about a verse form.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Clerihew Bentley invented the four-line comic biographical verse named after his middle name; the clue is written in that form.
explanation.definitionFit: The comic four-line rhyme about a person, with lines of uneven length, takes its name from Bentley's middle name.

clue.text: First place within reach for Fanny Burney

definitions.text: First place within reach for Fanny Burney

parts.words: First place within reach for Fanny Burney
parts.note: asks for Fanny Burney's birthplace, the first place she knew, a Norfolk port town

explanation.surface: The nearest spot available to the novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Burney was born in 1752 at King's Lynn, a port town in Norfolk, where her father was organist; that town was her first place.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Frances Burney was born at King's Lynn, so it is the first place in her life.

clue.text: Ruin mot produced by grandpa of Romulus

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are worked into something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clever remark spoils the old founder's grandfather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced' rearranges RUIN MOT; a mot is a witty saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Numitor, king of Alba Longa, was the father of Rhea Silvia and so the grandfather of Romulus and Remus.

clue.text: "Haggard" described his wife

parts.note: points to H. Rider Haggard's novel about the wife of his hunter hero

explanation.surface: A worn-out man's spouse is portrayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' looks like an adjective but is H. Rider Haggard, who wrote Allan's Wife about the hunter Allan Quatermain.
explanation.definitionFit: Allan Quatermain is Rider Haggard's hunter, and Allan's Wife tells of his marriage.

clue.text: Emily St Aubert's maid acquired from Caldwell?

parts.words: Emily St Aubert's maid acquired from Caldwell?
parts.note: asks for the servant of the heroine of The Mysteries of Udolpho, a name also borne by a Caldwell character

explanation.surface: A gothic heroine's servant was taken from another author.
explanation.walkthrough: Emily St Aubert is the heroine of Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho, and her chattering maid is Annette.
explanation.definitionFit: Annette is the talkative maid who attends Emily at the castle in Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho.

clue.text: Ambler's relaxation?

parts.note: an ambler is one who walks slowly, and also the thriller writer Eric Ambler

explanation.surface: How the thriller writer Eric Ambler unwinds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ambler' reads as Eric Ambler, the spy novelist, but is anyone who ambles, whose leisurely walk is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A leisurely walk is the restful pastime of one who ambles.

clue.text: It was put about by Adamson

definitions.text: It was put about by Adamson

parts.words: It was put about by Adamson
parts.note: something put about is spread by word of mouth; the title is a book by an Adamson

explanation.surface: A story was spread by a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Something 'put about' is gossip spread around; the title by an Adamson is a work called Rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay that is put about is talk spread from person to person.

clue.text: Time of greybeard's dropped hand

parts.note: the greybeard is Coleridge's Ancient Mariner, of whom it is said that soon after, 'his hand dropt he'

explanation.surface: When an old man let his arm fall.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Rime of the Ancient Mariner the wedding guest is held until 'Eftsoons his hand dropt he'; the greybeard is the Mariner.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word means soon after or forthwith, the moment at which the Mariner releases his grip.

clue.text: Response expected by a pair at the altar

definitions.text: Response expected by a pair at the altar

parts.words: Response expected by a pair at the altar
parts.note: reads as a couple's wedding vow but means a sung reply between two choirs in church

explanation.surface: The words a bride and groom are expected to say.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair at the altar looks like a marrying couple; it is two halves of a choir singing alternate responses.
explanation.definitionFit: A sung reply between two groups in a church service, chanted alternately.

clue.text: Woman of Sardou, or Crécy, always in Swann's way

definitions.text: Woman of Sardou, or Crécy, always in Swann's way

parts.words: Woman of Sardou, or Crécy, always in Swann's way
parts.note: names a heroine of a Sardou play and Proust's Mme de Crécy, who obsesses Swann

explanation.surface: A woman always getting in a gentleman's path.
explanation.walkthrough: Sardou wrote a play of this name, and Odette de Crécy is the courtesan in Proust's Swann's Way, always on Swann's mind; 'in Swann's way' also reads as obstructing him.
explanation.definitionFit: Odette is the name of Sardou's heroine and of Odette de Crécy, Swann's lover in Proust.

clue.text: Muir's place. Or a corner for Maugham?

definitions.text: Muir's place. Or a corner for Maugham?

parts.words: Muir's place. Or a corner for Maugham?
parts.note: Edwin Muir's collection and Somerset Maugham's novel share the same adjective in their titles

explanation.surface: Asks where a poet lives and which corner a novelist takes.
explanation.walkthrough: Edwin Muir's book is The Narrow Place and Somerset Maugham's novel is The Narrow Corner.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective meaning tight or slim opens both Muir's and Maugham's titles.

clue.text: Surprisingly realigns novelist

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters of the next word fall out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Lining things up again reveals an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surprisingly' rearranges REALIGNS; J. D. Salinger wrote The Catcher in the Rye.
explanation.definitionFit: J. D. Salinger is the American author of The Catcher in the Rye.
